memory_candidates.content: Linux's MAX_ARG_STRLEN (131,072-byte single-argument execve() ceiling) applies to EVERY process invocation, not just the terminal command you're worried about. A caller invoking `bash some_script.sh --argjson NAME "$HUGE_VALUE"` hits this ceiling at the OUTER bash invocation itself if $HUGE_VALUE exceeds ~131KB -- the target script's own internal argv-forwarding fix (e.g. spilling to jq --slurpfile before calling jq) never even runs, because the script's process can't be spawned with that argv in the first place. The only mechanism that genuinely accepts an unbounded single-call payload is one where the caller writes the payload to a file FIRST (inside its own already-running process, no new exec involved) and passes a short file-path argv token instead (e.g. an additive --argjson-file NAME PATH flag using jq --slurpfile). Before believing an internal-to-the-script argv fix resolves a >128KB-payload defect end-to-end, test the OUTER invocation with the oversized value literally on its own command line -- don't assume the fix's own internal logic is reachable.

git-snapshot.sh's DEFAULT mode reverts the working tree (git stash push -u) -- in a repo with concurrent orchestrator/agent activity, running it in default mode can stash away OTHER sessions' unrelated in-flight state.json/TODO.md/log changes, not just your own task's work, because the stash captures the ENTIRE dirty tree indiscriminately. When any concurrent process might be touching the same repo, always use `--no-revert` (a durable backup with zero working-tree mutation) instead of the default/--branch modes, and check `git status --short` before AND immediately after any snapshot call to catch an accidental broad-scope stash early -- it can be corrected via `git stash pop` if caught immediately, but the safe default is --no-revert from the start whenever live/concurrent machinery is a stated constraint.
